Chapter 11

Frequently Asked Questions

On this page

Here are some questions that come up when choosing or building a MoQ system. You can jump to whichever one you’re wondering about.

You can read this chapter in any order. For a term rather than a design question, use the glossary.

Is MoQ a finished standard?

Not yet. This book follows draft-ietf-moq-transport-21, dated September 8, 2026. Before implementing it, check the IETF document status for newer revisions.

The draft links point to the version this book explains. Project documentation may have moved on since then.

Does MoQ replace WebRTC?

You can use MoQ for some of the same jobs. Whether you’d want to depends on what you’re building. Start with the WebRTC comparison.

Our lecture has both a conversation and a broadcast: a student talks with the lecturer while everyone else listens. You could use WebRTC or MoQ as part of a system that handles both.

In a browser, WebRTC provides much of the encoding, transmission, and receiving machinery together. A MoQ implementation supplies named-content delivery; its media library supplies the capture, codec, and playback pieces above it. Compare complete systems on the devices and network paths your audience uses. The protocol name alone does not tell you the delay or operating cost.

Does it replace HLS or DASH?

HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) and DASH (Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP) describe ways for players to obtain media in pieces over HTTP, the protocol used for web requests. A description of the available media tells the player which pieces to request. This fits established web servers and caching infrastructure. The DASH Industry Forum’s architecture overview describes DASH’s presentation description and segment model.

MoQ instead lets a receiver subscribe to a named track and receive objects as they become available. Both approaches need media formats, players, and a policy for adapting to the network. Neither the use of HTTP nor subscription by itself fixes the final playback delay. HLS’s playlist-and-segment model is described in RFC 8216, section 2; MoQ subscriptions are described in draft-21, section 3.1.

You can also connect delivery systems through a gateway. The moq.dev project includes gateways for other formats and protocols. Check that the one you choose supports the media you want to send.

Why would I cancel a reliable stream?

Because you might not want those bytes anymore. If the viewer is behind and a newer group gives them a fresh place to start, finishing the old group keeps them waiting. The sender can cancel that work and keep using reliable delivery for the content the viewer still needs.

The receiver also needs to discard its stale playback queue and resume at a valid point. Cancellation alone cannot make a player catch up. Latency and Congestion follows those decisions.

This also answers a common question: is all MoQ traffic unreliable? No. An active QUIC stream provides reliable, ordered bytes. Datagrams are a separate option: QUIC does not retransmit them when they are lost. QUIC and WebTransport explains the distinction.

Can I send chat or game state?

Yes. Think about what a late arrival or a lost update means for your data. A new snapshot of the game state can replace an old one. An “increment score” event needs the earlier score to make sense.

For example, a game could start each group with a full snapshot and follow it with updates. If you need to keep every event, you’ll also need storage and a way to recover anything missed.

Is MoQ peer-to-peer?

In the browser setup used here, the publisher and viewers connect to a relay over WebTransport. They don’t connect directly to each other, and MOQT doesn’t provide ICE, STUN, or TURN for NAT traversal.

MOQT can still carry content directly between two endpoints that can reach each other. Native software can add its own peer connectivity, as moq.dev describes. That connectivity comes from the surrounding stack. For our lecture, relays also solve the scaling problem: the lecturer sends one copy and the servers handle distribution to the audience.

Is moq-lite the same as MOQT?

No. moq-lite uses a simpler model. The moq.dev stack also supports some MOQT versions and features. To connect it to another implementation, check the version, features, and media format on both sides.

Can I use this book as a specification?

Use the book to learn how the pieces work. When implementing them, follow the protocol draft and the documentation for your library version. The references explain which versions this edition uses.
